slides.say: The balance also helps with calculations. Let's find the average of ninety-seven, a hundred two, a hundred four and ninety-nine.
We don't add them up. These numbers are all near a hundred. So we pick a hundred as a base, and we write only the differences.
Ninety-seven is three below, so minus three. A hundred two is two above, so plus two. A hundred four is four above, so plus four. Ninety-nine is one below, so minus one.
The minuses are minus three and minus one. Together, that's minus four.
The pluses are two and four. Together, that's plus six.
Together, six minus four is plus two. So the four numbers have two extra above the base.
Shared among four numbers, two divided by four is one half.
So the average is a hundred plus one half, a hundred and a half.

slides: So when the numbers are close to a round number, use it as a base. The numbers stay small, so we make fewer mistakes.

slides.say: Now what happens when one value changes? Five students took a test. One score goes up by ten points.
The sum goes up by ten. There are still five scores, so we share the ten among them.
Ten divided by five is two. So the average goes up by two points.

slides: And we didn't need any of the scores. The change in the sum is shared among all the values.
